events.description: Test your understanding of modern Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Generative models in 5 quick questions.

questions.question: If an AI model achieves 99.8% accuracy on your training dataset, but performs worse than a coin toss on fresh test data, what is most likely happening?
questions.option_a: The model has achieved Artificial Superintelligence and is rebelling.
questions.option_b: Severe overfitting — it memorized training noise instead of general patterns.
questions.option_c: Underfitting — it did not train for enough epochs.
questions.option_d: The GPU overheated and flipped random floating-point bits.
questions.explanation: Overfitting occurs when a model memorizes quirks and noise in the training dataset rather than learning generalizable underlying patterns. It looks like a genius on homework, but fails on the real exam!

questions.question: When a Large Language Model writes a totally fabricated, yet extraordinarily confident citation of an academic research paper that does not exist, this phenomenon is called:
questions.option_a: Model Dreaming
questions.option_b: Hallucination
questions.option_c: Vector Drift
questions.option_d: Gradient Explosion
questions.explanation: Hallucination in LLMs occurs when models produce plausible-sounding but factually untrue information. LLMs predict statistically likely word sequences, not verified facts.

questions.question: In modern Transformer architectures (the engine behind modern LLMs), what does the "Attention Mechanism" fundamentally do?
questions.option_a: It penalizes students who glance away from their screens during proctored exams.
questions.option_b: It calculates dynamic weights representing how much each token relates to every other token.
questions.option_c: It caches web responses to save electricity in Google datacenters.
questions.option_d: It prevents the GPU from entering sleep mode during gradient descent.
questions.explanation: The Self-Attention mechanism allows models to dynamically weigh the importance and contextual relevance of different words in a sentence, regardless of their distance apart.

questions.question: What is the key practical distinction between "Narrow AI" and "Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)"?
questions.option_a: Narrow AI runs on phones; AGI requires alien quantum supercomputers.
questions.option_b: Narrow AI excels at a specialized task; AGI can flexibly learn and solve any intellectual task a human can.
questions.option_c: Narrow AI is programmed in Python; AGI can only be compiled from C++.
questions.option_d: Narrow AI only works in dark mode.
questions.explanation: All AI today (AlphaGo, ChatGPT, Tesla Autopilot) is Narrow AI designed for specific tasks. AGI is a theoretical system capable of general reasoning across any domain like a human.

questions.question: A real-world autonomous car abruptly slammed its brakes on an open highway because it repeatedly mistook the low yellow harvest moon for a traffic light. What type of ML issue is this?
questions.option_a: Steering wheel firmware corruption.
questions.option_b: An Out-of-Distribution (OOD) visual edge case.
questions.option_c: Satellite GPS clock skew.
questions.option_d: The autonomous car felt tired and needed coffee.
questions.explanation: True story! Machine learning computer vision models struggle with Out-of-Distribution (OOD) edge cases—rare visual scenarios never properly represented in their training data.

questions.question: What happens when you set the "Temperature" parameter to 0.0 when querying a Large Language Model?
questions.option_a: The datacenter fans shut down immediately.
questions.option_b: The output becomes strictly greedy and deterministic (choosing the highest probability token).
questions.option_c: The API call becomes free of charge.
questions.option_d: The model switches entirely into pirate speech mode.
questions.explanation: Temperature controls output randomness. At 0.0, the model deterministically selects the top probability token at each step, making it ideal for math, JSON schema, and coding.

questions.question: Why are Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) drastically better than standard Multi-Layer Perceptrons for computer vision tasks?
questions.option_a: MLPs cannot read 24-bit PNG image files.
questions.option_b: CNNs preserve 2D spatial locality and drastically reduce parameters using sliding shared kernels.
questions.option_c: CNNs bypass backpropagation and matrix operations.
questions.option_d: Convolution is a proprietary feature exclusive to NVIDIA drivers.
questions.explanation: CNNs exploit spatial hierarchy: nearby pixels are related. By sharing weights across sliding convolution filters, they detect edges, textures, and objects with far fewer weights.

questions.question: In modern Natural Language Processing and Search, what is a "Vector Embedding"?
questions.option_a: A secret invisible copyright watermark embedded in generated essays.
questions.option_b: A list of high-dimensional numbers where semantically similar concepts cluster close together.
questions.option_c: A CSS class used to format HTML paragraphs in rich text editors.
questions.option_d: A compression scheme that strips vowels from database tables.
questions.explanation: Vector embeddings map words, sentences, or images into mathematical vector spaces. Items with similar semantic meanings have small cosine distances (e.g., "doctor" is near "hospital").

questions.question: You are training a deep neural network and suddenly your loss displays "NaN" on epoch 4. What is the most common culprit?
questions.option_a: The server ran out of prime numbers.
questions.option_b: Exploding gradients caused by an excessively high learning rate.
questions.option_c: The student cafeteria microwave disrupted the WiFi router.
questions.option_d: Python garbage collector deleted the target tensors.
questions.explanation: Exploding gradients occur when gradients accumulate exponentially during backpropagation, leading to numerical overflow (infinity), which NumPy and PyTorch represent as NaN.

questions.question: What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) in modern AI application architecture?
questions.option_a: A technique to randomly shuffle training samples.
questions.option_b: A technique that retrieves relevant external facts/documents and feeds them to the LLM to ground its answer.
questions.option_c: A hardware accelerator chip produced by Intel.
questions.option_d: An automated testing tool for React frontend components.
questions.explanation: RAG connects LLMs to your private or fresh knowledge base: it searches a vector database for relevant documentation snippets and passes them into the prompt, preventing hallucinations.

questions.question: What was the foundational objective of the "Turing Test" proposed by Alan Turing in 1950?
questions.option_a: To test whether an algorithm could beat Garry Kasparov in chess.
questions.option_b: To test whether an interrogator can distinguish a computer's responses from those of a human.
questions.option_c: To calculate the cryptographic security of public key RSA algorithms.
questions.option_d: To verify whether a computer program halts or loops forever.
questions.explanation: Alan Turing proposed the "Imitation Game", exploring whether an artificial agent could generate natural text responses indistinguishable from a real human being.

questions.question: For an AI system screening patients for a life-threatening, contagious disease, which metric is most vital to prioritize?
questions.option_a: High Recall (Sensitivity) — minimizing False Negatives so no sick patient goes undetected.
questions.option_b: Low CPU temperature on the hospital server.
questions.option_c: High Dropout rate to reduce the model size by 95%.
questions.option_d: Training speed measured in milliseconds per batch.
questions.explanation: In medical screening, a False Negative (telling a sick person they are healthy) is catastrophic. High Recall ensures virtually all positive cases are identified for treatment.

questions.question: Why do modern LLMs tokenize text into subwords (e.g. Byte-Pair Encoding) instead of using raw entire words or single characters?
questions.option_a: Because ASCII only has 128 characters.
questions.option_b: Subword tokenization balances vocabulary size, handles typos & rare words gracefully, and optimizes compression.
questions.option_c: Tokens are physical arcade tokens inserted into NVIDIA server racks.
questions.option_d: It was mandated by international telecom standards in 1998.
questions.explanation: Subwords let models keep frequent words as single tokens while decomposing unfamiliar words, neologisms, and code syntax into smaller chunks without needing an infinite dictionary.

questions.question: How do modern Image Diffusion models (such as Imagen or Stable Diffusion) produce photographic images from text prompts?
questions.option_a: They run a Google Image search and collage pixels together.
questions.option_b: They start from random Gaussian noise and iteratively subtract predicted noise guided by text embeddings.
questions.option_c: They run Unreal Engine 5 in headless cloud instances.
questions.option_d: They compute the Fourier transform of the audio pronunciation of the words.
questions.explanation: Diffusion models are trained to reverse a thermodynamic-like degradation process: given pure static noise, they iteratively remove noise step-by-step until a sharp image appears.

questions.question: A large tech company developed an AI recruiting tool trained on 10 years of historical resumes, and it started penalizing female candidates. Why did this happen?
questions.option_a: A syntax error in an if/else conditional check.
questions.option_b: Historical bias present in the training dataset reflected past male-dominated hiring patterns.
questions.option_c: The training computer was running on 32-bit architecture.
questions.option_d: The candidates submitted their resumes in PDF instead of DOCX.
questions.explanation: This was an infamous real-world case (Amazon 2018). Machine learning models mirror the biases inherent in historical data unless deliberately mitigated and audited.

questions.question: What is the fundamental purpose of the "Loss Function" in training an AI model?
questions.option_a: To log the monetary cost of electricity used by cloud GPUs.
questions.option_b: To calculate a numerical penalty representing how far the model's prediction is from ground truth.
questions.option_c: To measure how many lines of legacy code were deprecated.
questions.option_d: To discard underperforming nodes in the database cluster.
questions.explanation: The loss function mathematically scores prediction error. Optimizers calculate the gradient of this loss function with respect to weights to know how to adjust parameters.

questions.question: What is the operational difference between "Image Classification" and "Object Detection"?
questions.option_a: Classification predicts what is in the overall image; Detection predicts what is present AND where (with bounding boxes).
questions.option_b: Classification only works on monochrome images; Detection works on color.
questions.option_c: Classification is supervised; Detection is purely unsupervised.
questions.option_d: They are identical marketing terms with no technical distinction.
questions.explanation: Image classification assigns a label to the whole image ("this is a dog"). Object detection identifies multiple objects and pinpoints their spatial bounding box coordinates.

questions.question: What is "Fine-Tuning" of a pre-trained foundation model?
questions.option_a: Adjusting monitor contrast and display refresh rate.
questions.option_b: Taking a broad pre-trained model and training it further on specialized target-domain data.
questions.option_c: Deleting 90% of model weights to fit into an embedded microcontroller.
questions.option_d: Manually translating Python weights into C++ header files.
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning leverages transfer learning: taking a general model trained on trillions of web tokens and slightly tuning its weights on specialized data (e.g. legal docs or medical chats).

questions.question: What is RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)?
questions.option_a: Spamming angry emails to developers when a chatbot hallucinates.
questions.option_b: Using human rankings of model outputs to train a reward model that guides the LLM toward helpful, harmless answers.
questions.option_c: A physical test measuring human typing speed against an AI.
questions.option_d: Running captcha challenges on login pages.
questions.explanation: RLHF is the alignment technique that transformed raw completion models into conversational assistants (like ChatGPT & Claude) by training them against human preferences.

questions.question: Why can an AI model achieving 100% accuracy on a closed benchmark still fail in production?
questions.option_a: The real world is dynamic, noisy, subject to concept drift, and filled with unseen edge cases.
questions.option_b: Real-world gravity interferes with silicon transistors.
questions.option_c: IEEE standards prohibit 100% accuracy in public networks.
questions.option_d: JavaScript runtimes introduce rounding bugs in floating-point operations.
questions.explanation: Static benchmark tests do not represent the chaotic, non-stationary nature of the real world. Models encounter covariate shift, adversarial inputs, and unexpected corner cases.
